case_name: Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Pinkcity Midway Petroleums
facts: A dispute arose between HPCL and Pinkcity regarding a dealership agreement. The agreement contained an arbitration clause. HPCL terminated the dealership, and Pinkcity challenged the termination. The question arose whether the arbitration clause survived the termination of the underlying contract.
issues: Whether an arbitration clause survives the termination of the underlying contract
Doctrine of separability of the arbitration agreement
Scope of Section 16 of the Arbitration Act
arguments: The appellant argued that termination of the contract extinguished all clauses including arbitration. The respondent contended that the arbitration agreement is independent and survives termination under the doctrine of separability.
reasoning: The Court held that an arbitration agreement is a separate agreement from the underlying contract. The doctrine of separability means that the arbitration clause can survive even when the main contract is terminated, rescinded, or declared void.
holding: An arbitration agreement is independent of and separate from the underlying contract. Termination of the contract does not ipso facto terminate the arbitration agreement.

case_name: NTPC Ltd. v. Singer Company
facts: NTPC entered into a contract with Singer Company for supply of equipment. A dispute arose and NTPC sought to invoke arbitration. Singer contested the jurisdiction arguing the contract was frustrated.
issues: Whether frustration of the main contract affects the arbitration clause
Autonomous nature of the arbitration agreement
Relationship between arbitration clause and main contract
arguments: Singer argued that frustration of the contract rendered the arbitration clause inoperative. NTPC argued the arbitration clause was autonomous and survived.
reasoning: The Supreme Court recognized the principle that an arbitration clause is a separate and autonomous agreement. It does not perish with the termination or frustration of the main contract in which it is contained.
holding: An arbitration clause is a collateral and autonomous agreement. It does not get extinguished by the frustration or termination of the main contract.

case_name: Reva Electric Car Company Pvt. Ltd. v. Green Mobil
facts: Reva Electric entered into a distribution agreement with Green Mobil containing an arbitration clause. The agreement was subsequently terminated. Green Mobil filed a civil suit. Reva sought reference to arbitration under Section 8.
issues: Whether Section 8 reference is maintainable after contract termination
Doctrine of separability under the 1996 Act
arguments: Green Mobil argued that with the termination of the contract, the arbitration clause ceased to exist. Reva contended the arbitration clause survives termination.
reasoning: The Court applied the doctrine of separability, holding that the arbitration agreement has an independent existence. The termination of the contract does not ipso facto terminate the arbitration agreement contained therein.
holding: The arbitration agreement, being a separate agreement, survives the termination of the main contract. The kompetenz-kompetenz principle under Section 16 empowers the tribunal to rule on its own jurisdiction.

case_name: Chloro Controls India Pvt. Ltd. v. Severn Trent Water Purification Inc.
facts: Multiple agreements existed between the parties, some containing arbitration clauses and some not. The dispute arose across multiple contracts. The question was whether non-signatories could be bound by arbitration agreements in related contracts.
issues: Extension of arbitration agreement to non-signatories
arguments: The respondent argued for applying the group of companies doctrine to bind non-signatory affiliates to the arbitration agreement.
reasoning: The Court recognized the group of companies doctrine, holding that the corporate veil can be pierced when companies within a group have a tight group structure and one company can be bound by the arbitration clause agreed to by another in the group.
holding: The group of companies doctrine permits extension of the arbitration agreement to non-signatory parties within the same corporate group when the circumstances demonstrate mutual intention and intertwined obligations.

case_name: Bhatia International v. Bulk Trading S.A.
facts: Bhatia International and Bulk Trading had disputes arising from international commodity trade. The seat of arbitration was Paris. Bhatia approached Indian courts seeking interim relief under Part I of the Act.
issues: Applicability of Part I of the Arbitration Act to international commercial arbitrations seated outside India
Territorial scope of the Arbitration Act
arguments: Bulk Trading argued Part I applies only to domestic arbitrations. Bhatia contended Part I provisions are applicable unless expressly or impliedly excluded.
reasoning: The Court held that Part I of the Arbitration Act applies to all arbitrations including international commercial arbitrations held outside India, unless the parties by agreement, express or implied, exclude its applicability.
holding: Part I of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 applies to international commercial arbitrations held outside India unless excluded by agreement of the parties.

case_name: Bharat Aluminium Co. v. Kaiser Aluminium Technical Services Inc. (BALCO)
facts: BALCO entered into a contract with Kaiser for technical services. Disputes arose and were referred to arbitration seated outside India. BALCO challenged the award under Section 34 in Indian courts.
arguments: Kaiser argued that Bhatia International was incorrectly decided and Part I should apply only to arbitrations seated in India.
reasoning: The Constitution Bench overruled Bhatia International, holding that Part I of the Act applies only when the place of arbitration is in India. The seat of arbitration determines the applicable law.
holding: Part I of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 is applicable only to arbitrations having their seat/place in India. Bhatia International overruled prospectively.

case_name: Vidya Drolia v. Durga Trading Corporation
facts: Durga Trading filed a suit for eviction against its tenant. Vidya Drolia sought reference to arbitration relying on an arbitration clause in the tenancy agreement. The question was whether landlord-tenant disputes are arbitrable.
issues: Court's role at the referral stage under Section 8
arguments: Vidya Drolia argued all disputes with an arbitration agreement should be referred to arbitration. Durga Trading contended landlord-tenant disputes are non-arbitrable.
reasoning: The Court laid down a comprehensive test for non-arbitrability based on: (1) cause of action and subject matter of the dispute, (2) the nature of rights involved, (3) whether adjudication creates rights in rem, and (4) whether the dispute involves sovereign functions.
holding: Landlord-tenant disputes governed by special statutes where the tenant enjoys statutory protection are non-arbitrable. The Court laid down a four-fold test for determining arbitrability.

case_name: Ssangyong Engineering & Construction Co. Ltd. v. NHAI
facts: Ssangyong challenged an arbitral award before the Delhi High Court. The case reached the Supreme Court on the scope of judicial review under Section 34 of the amended Act.
issues: Meaning of public policy of India
arguments: NHAI argued for broad judicial review. Ssangyong argued the court's role is limited under Section 34.
reasoning: The Court clarified the scope of public policy challenge under Section 34, holding that the 2015 amendment narrowed the ground significantly. Patent illegality must go to the root of the matter.
holding: Post-2015 amendment, the public policy ground under Section 34 is restricted. Patent illegality is available only for domestic awards and must go to the root of the matter, not merely errors of law.

case_name: Associate Builders v. Delhi Development Authority
facts: DDA awarded a construction contract to Associate Builders. Disputes arose and were referred to arbitration. DDA challenged the award under Section 34.
issues: Scope of judicial interference with arbitral awards
Public policy of India under Section 34
Perversity as a ground for challenge
arguments: DDA argued the award was contrary to public policy and perverse. Associate Builders argued for minimal judicial interference.
reasoning: The Court held that an award can be set aside on the ground of patent illegality or if the finding is perverse, meaning no reasonable person could have arrived at such a conclusion.
holding: A finding of fact can be challenged under Section 34 only if it is perverse — that is, based on no evidence, or if the arbitrator ignored vital evidence, or if the view taken is not even a possible view.

case_name: Duro Felguera S.A. v. Gangavaram Port Ltd.
facts: Gangavaram Port and Duro Felguera had disputes under an EPC contract. The question arose about the scope of the court's enquiry at the referral stage.
issues: Scope of judicial enquiry under Section 11
Prima facie examination of arbitration agreement
arguments: Duro Felguera argued for limited judicial enquiry. Gangavaram sought a full examination of the arbitration agreement's validity.
reasoning: The Court held that after the 2015 amendment, the scope of judicial enquiry at the referral stage is confined to examining the existence of the arbitration agreement. Other issues should be left to the arbitral tribunal.
holding: Post-2015 amendment, the court at the referral stage (Section 8/11) is required only to examine the existence of an arbitration agreement and nothing more. All other objections are for the tribunal.

case_name: Perkins Eastman Architects DPC v. HSCC (India) Ltd.
facts: HSCC had an arbitration clause providing that a person nominated by its CMD would be the sole arbitrator. Perkins Eastman challenged this as lacking impartiality.
issues: Independence and impartiality of arbitral tribunal
arguments: Perkins argued that a unilateral appointment mechanism violates principles of equal treatment. HSCC contended the clause should be given effect.
reasoning: The Court held that party autonomy cannot override the fundamental requirement of independence and impartiality. An arbitration clause that allows one party to unilaterally appoint the arbitrator is invalid.
holding: A clause that gives one party the unilateral right to appoint a sole arbitrator is invalid as it violates principles of independence and impartiality under Section 12.

case_name: Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer
facts: In an election dispute, the appellant relied on audio and video recordings to prove corrupt practices. The electronic evidence was produced without compliance with Section 65B certificate requirements.
issues: Overruling of previous position on electronic evidence
arguments: P.K. Basheer argued that electronic evidence without Section 65B certificate is inadmissible. Anvar contended substantial compliance was sufficient.
reasoning: The Court held that Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act provides a complete code for admissibility of electronic records. The requirement of a certificate under Section 65B(4) is mandatory.
holding: Electronic evidence is admissible only if accompanied by a certificate under Section 65B(4) of the Indian Evidence Act. The certificate requirement is mandatory, not directory.

case_name: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal
facts: In an election petition, video recordings were produced. The question of compliance with Section 65B requirements and the scope of the Anvar P.V. judgment arose.
issues: Clarification of Anvar P.V. on Section 65B
When is Section 65B certificate not required
Producer of original electronic device exception
arguments: Khotkar argued that the original device holder need not produce a 65B certificate. Gorantyal relied on strict Anvar P.V. requirements.
reasoning: The Court clarified that the requirement of Section 65B(4) certificate is mandatory. However, if the original electronic device itself is produced before the court, a Section 65B certificate is not required.
holding: Section 65B(4) certificate is mandatory for secondary electronic evidence. However, if the party produces the original device from which the electronic record is generated, Section 65B certification is not required.

case_name: Shafhi Mohammad v. State of Himachal Pradesh
facts: Mobile phone video footage of an incident was sought to be admitted as evidence. The question of requirement of Section 65B certificate for mobile phone recordings arose.
issues: Applicability of Section 65B to mobile phone recordings
When certificate requirement may be relaxed
arguments: The accused argued Section 65B compliance was mandatory for mobile evidence. The State argued for a pragmatic approach.
reasoning: The Court adopted a pragmatic approach, noting that rigid insistence on Section 65B certificate for every piece of electronic evidence may defeat the ends of justice. However, this was later clarified by the larger bench in Arjun Panditrao.
holding: The requirement of Section 65B certificate should be applied with pragmatism. However, this ruling was effectively clarified by the three-judge bench in Arjun Panditrao Khotkar.

case_name: Trimex International FZE Ltd. v. Vedanta Aluminium Ltd.
facts: Disputes arose between Trimex and Vedanta regarding a contract for supply of aluminium. The question was whether email exchanges and conduct of parties could establish a binding contractual relationship in the absence of a formally signed agreement.
issues: Formation of contract through electronic communications
Conduct as evidence of contractual relationship
Implied contract from course of dealing
arguments: Trimex argued that email exchanges and subsequent conduct established a binding contract. Vedanta argued no formal contract was ever signed.
reasoning: The Court held that a contract need not be in a formal written document. It can be inferred from the conduct of parties, correspondence, and surrounding circumstances. Electronic communications can constitute valid contractual communications.
holding: A contractual relationship can be established through electronic communications, conduct of parties, and surrounding circumstances even in the absence of a formally executed written contract.

case_name: Tomaso Bruno v. State of Uttar Pradesh
facts: An Italian national was tried for murder. The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence including forensic evidence, electronic records, and witness testimony.
issues: Standard of proof for circumstantial evidence
Role of forensic and electronic evidence
arguments: The defense argued circumstantial evidence was insufficient. The prosecution argued the chain of circumstances was complete.
reasoning: The Court reiterated the principles of circumstantial evidence — the chain must be complete, pointing to the guilt of the accused and inconsistent with innocence. Each circumstance must be proved beyond reasonable doubt.
holding: Circumstantial evidence can form the basis for conviction if the chain of circumstances is complete, unerringly points to the guilt of the accused, and is inconsistent with the hypothesis of innocence.

case_name: Ram Singh v. Col. Ram Singh
facts: A property dispute between family members where oral evidence was sought to be led to contradict the terms of a written agreement.
issues: Parol evidence rule under Sections 91 and 92
When oral evidence can supplement or contradict written agreements
Exceptions to the parol evidence rule
arguments: One party sought to lead oral evidence to vary the written terms. The other invoked Sections 91-92.
reasoning: The Court applied the parol evidence rule strictly, holding that when the terms of a contract have been reduced to writing, no evidence can be given to contradict, vary, or add to those terms.
holding: Under Sections 91 and 92 of the Indian Evidence Act, when a contract is reduced to writing, oral evidence cannot be admitted to contradict or vary its terms, subject to recognized exceptions.

case_name: State of NCT of Delhi v. Navjot Sandhu (Parliament Attack Case)
facts: In the Parliament attack case, mobile phone call records and electronic evidence were relied upon by the prosecution. The admissibility of electronic records without strict Section 65B compliance was in question.
issues: Admissibility of call records as electronic evidence
arguments: The defense challenged the admissibility of call records without proper Section 65B certification. The prosecution argued for liberal interpretation.
reasoning: The Court took a liberal view on admissibility of electronic evidence, holding that the requirement of certificate under Section 65B is procedural and not substantive. This view was later overruled by Anvar P.V.
holding: Electronic evidence including call records can be admitted without strict Section 65B compliance when produced under Section 63/65 as secondary evidence. [Note: This position was overruled by Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer (2014)]

case_name: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India
facts: A challenge to the Aadhaar scheme raised the fundamental question of whether the right to privacy is a constitutionally protected fundamental right. The Attorney General argued that privacy was not a fundamental right based on earlier decisions.
issues: Whether the right to privacy is a fundamental right
Overruling of M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh on privacy
arguments: The petitioners argued privacy is intrinsic to liberty and dignity under Article 21. The Union argued privacy was not an independently guaranteed fundamental right.
reasoning: The nine-judge bench unanimously held that the right to privacy is a constitutionally protected fundamental right. Privacy is an intrinsic part of life and personal liberty under Article 21 and also flows from other fundamental rights.
holding: The right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution.

case_name: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
facts: Maneka Gandhi's passport was impounded by the government without giving reasons. She challenged this action as violative of her fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19, and 21.
issues: What constitutes procedure established by law
arguments: The petitioner argued that impounding the passport without reasons violated Article 21. The government contended the Passport Act authorized the action.
reasoning: The Court expanded the scope of Article 21 by reading it along with Articles 14 and 19. It held that procedure established by law must be right, just and fair — not arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive.
holding: Articles 14, 19 and 21 are not mutually exclusive but form a trinity. Any procedure under Article 21 must be right, just and fair, effectively introducing due process into Indian constitutional law.

case_name: Kharak Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh
facts: Kharak Singh, a dacoit suspect, was subjected to domiciliary visits and surveillance under UP Police Regulations. He challenged this as violative of his fundamental rights.
arguments: Kharak Singh argued surveillance violated his right to privacy and personal liberty. The State argued police had regulatory power for crime prevention.
reasoning: The majority struck down domiciliary visits as unconstitutional but held that the right to privacy was not a guaranteed fundamental right. Justice Subba Rao in his minority opinion held that privacy is part of personal liberty.
holding: Domiciliary visits by police are unconstitutional as they violate Article 21. The majority held privacy was not a fundamental right, but the minority view (later vindicated in Puttaswamy) recognized privacy as part of personal liberty.

case_name: Selvi v. State of Karnataka
facts: The validity of narcoanalysis, polygraph, and brain-mapping tests administered involuntarily on accused persons was challenged as violative of the right against self-incrimination and personal liberty.
issues: Constitutionality of narcoanalysis and polygraph tests
arguments: The petitioners argued forced tests violate mental privacy and self-incrimination rights. The State argued these are scientific investigation tools.
reasoning: The Court held that involuntary administration of narcoanalysis, polygraph, and brain-mapping tests violates the right against self-incrimination under Article 20(3) and the right to personal liberty under Article 21.
holding: Narcoanalysis, polygraph, and brain-mapping tests cannot be administered involuntarily. They violate Article 20(3) and Article 21. Results of voluntary tests are admissible only as corroborative evidence.

case_name: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan
facts: A social worker was gang-raped in Rajasthan for attempting to prevent child marriage. In the absence of legislation, the Court was asked to lay down guidelines for prevention of sexual harassment at workplace.
issues: Sexual harassment as violation of fundamental rights
Judicial legislation in absence of statutory provisions
arguments: The petitioners argued for judicial intervention in the absence of legislation. The respondents argued law-making is Parliament's domain.
reasoning: The Court held that sexual harassment violates fundamental rights under Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21. In the absence of legislation, the Court exercised its power under Article 32 to lay down binding guidelines.
holding: Sexual harassment at the workplace violates fundamental rights. The Vishaka Guidelines were laid down as binding law until legislation is enacted. These were later superseded by the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013.

case_name: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
facts: A letter petition regarding custodial deaths prompted the Supreme Court to lay down guidelines to prevent custodial violence and torture.
arguments: The petitioner highlighted the prevalence of custodial deaths. The State argued existing safeguards were adequate.
reasoning: The Court held that custodial violence is a violation of Article 21 and laid down 11 requirements to be followed during arrest and detention.
holding: The Court laid down 11 mandatory guidelines for arrest and detention including: informing a relative, medical examination, memo of arrest, right to meet lawyer. Custodial torture violates Article 21.

case_name: K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (Aadhaar Judgment)
facts: After the nine-judge bench confirmed privacy as a fundamental right, the challenge to the Aadhaar Act was heard by a five-judge bench on its merits.
issues: Right to privacy and state surveillance
arguments: Petitioners argued Aadhaar violated privacy rights and was unconstitutionally passed as a money bill. The Union defended Aadhaar as enabling legitimate state interest.
reasoning: The majority upheld the core Aadhaar framework but struck down Section 57 (use by private entities) and Section 33(2) (national security exception without judicial oversight). Justice Chandrachud dissented on the money bill issue.
holding: Aadhaar Act is constitutionally valid for government subsidies and tax filing. Section 57 (private use of Aadhaar) struck down. Mandatory linking with bank accounts and mobile phones struck down.

case_name: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
facts: Kesavananda Bharati, the head of a religious mutt, challenged the Kerala Land Reforms Act. The larger question was whether Parliament's amending power under Article 368 was unlimited.
issues: Whether Parliament's amending power is unlimited
arguments: The State argued Parliament had unlimited amending power. The petitioner argued certain features of the Constitution cannot be amended.
reasoning: The Court by a 7-6 majority held that while Parliament has wide powers to amend the Constitution, it cannot alter the basic structure or essential features of the Constitution.
holding: Parliament's amending power under Article 368 does not include the power to destroy or abrogate the basic structure or framework of the Constitution. The basic structure doctrine was established.

case_name: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India
facts: Minerva Mills challenged the nationalization of its textile mill and the constitutional validity of the 42nd Amendment which sought to expand parliamentary power and curtail judicial review.
issues: Relationship between fundamental rights and directive principles
arguments: The Union argued the 42nd Amendment was valid exercise of constituent power. The petitioner argued it destroyed the basic structure.
reasoning: The Court struck down key provisions of the 42nd Amendment, holding that the balance between fundamental rights and directive principles is a basic feature that cannot be destroyed.
holding: Judicial review and the balance between fundamental rights and directive principles are part of the basic structure. The 42nd Amendment's attempt to make amendments non-justiciable was unconstitutional.

case_name: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu
facts: The validity of laws placed in the Ninth Schedule of the Constitution was challenged. The question was whether laws placed in the Ninth Schedule are immune from judicial review under the basic structure doctrine.
issues: Whether Ninth Schedule laws are immune from basic structure review
arguments: The State argued Ninth Schedule provides absolute immunity. The petitioners argued basic structure limits even Ninth Schedule protection.
reasoning: The Court held that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 (the date of Kesavananda Bharati) are open to challenge if they violate the basic structure, including fundamental rights.
holding: Laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 are amenable to judicial review and can be struck down if they violate the basic structure of the Constitution, including fundamental rights.

case_name: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
facts: Multiple state governments were dismissed under Article 356. The dismissed Chief Ministers challenged the Presidential proclamations as unconstitutional.
issues: Scope of judicial review of Article 356
arguments: The dismissed state governments argued Article 356 was misused for political purposes. The Centre argued the President's satisfaction is subjective and non-justiciable.
reasoning: The Court held that the presidential proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review. Secularism and federalism are part of the basic structure.
holding: Presidential proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review. The Court can examine whether the President's satisfaction was based on relevant material. Secularism is a basic feature of the Constitution.

case_name: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (Mandal Commission Case)
facts: The implementation of the Mandal Commission recommendations for 27% reservation in government jobs for Other Backward Classes was challenged.
arguments: The petitioners challenged reservations exceeding 50%. The Union defended the Mandal Commission recommendations.
reasoning: The Court upheld the 27% OBC reservation but imposed a 50% ceiling on total reservations. It introduced the creamy layer concept and held that economic criteria alone cannot define backward classes.
holding: Reservations under Articles 15(4) and 16(4) should not exceed 50% in aggregate. The creamy layer within backward classes must be excluded. Caste can be a starting point for identifying backward classes.

case_name: Waman Rao v. Union of India
facts: The petitioner challenged land reform legislation placed in the Ninth Schedule. The question was the scope of Ninth Schedule immunity vis-à-vis the basic structure doctrine.
issues: Ninth Schedule protection and basic structure
arguments: The petitioner argued Ninth Schedule laws violating basic structure should be reviewable. The State argued absolute immunity.
reasoning: The Court held that amendments to the Ninth Schedule made after the date of Kesavananda Bharati are open to challenge on the ground that they damage the basic structure.
holding: Constitutional amendments including those adding laws to the Ninth Schedule, made on or after April 24, 1973, are open to challenge on the basis of the basic structure doctrine.
